factions.name: The Brine-Factors (the Salt Exchange)
factions.battleCry: "Everything's for sale before the Toll — and so are you."

lore.origin: The Brine-Factors did not begin as archivists at all. They were the salvage-crews and bilge-runners who skimmed the receding margins for whatever the other three orders left behind — cracked salt-glass too damaged to enshrine, off-cuts the Mnemarchs deemed unsanctifiable, shards the Iconoclasts hadn't gotten around to breaking. They were scavengers of scavengers. The turn came when a wading hauler named Cassine Lir re-lived a half-spoiled crystal of a battle that had never been fought, edited the salt so it read as a great Mnemarch victory, and sold that lie back to the Mnemarchs themselves for a skiff's weight in unspoiled brine. She had discovered the one thing the other orders refused to admit: a memory is worth not what happened, but what someone will pay to have happened. The First Ledger was opened that afternoon. By the time the Concord Litany shattered, the Factors had already insured both sides of the truce and collected on the breach. They were the only order to profit from the peace's unmaking.
lore.culture: A mercantile guild dressed as a religion of the deal, or a religion dressed as a guild — the Factors themselves no longer bother to distinguish, since the distinction doesn't price differently. Every Factor carries a ledger-stone, a slab of dark salt-glass on which their debts and credits are crystallized; to die owing more than you're owed is the only true Factor disgrace, and the dead are appraised before they are mourned. They speak in the cant of the Exchange: a friend is a 'counterparty,' a death is a 'write-off,' a lie well sold is 'a clean book.' They have a horror, almost physical, of holding ground — to be stationary is to be unleveraged, and an unleveraged Factor is a Factor about to be liquidated by someone faster. They are charming, profoundly untrustworthy, and the only people on the flat who laugh, because they are the only ones who have decided the apocalypse is a market opportunity rather than a tragedy. They drink iodine-cut brine on purpose to blur which memories are theirs, on the theory that a clear conscience is just unrealized inventory.
lore.whyTheyFight: They fight because the Sea is the final liquidation sale of all history, and a closing sale waits for no one. The Mnemarchs want to fix the past, the Iconoclasts to erase it, the Sediment to free it — all of which, to a Factor, are different ways of taking inventory off the market and destroying its value. The Factors fight to keep the past liquid, tradeable, and theirs to price, right up until the Toll strikes dry. They do not especially want any particular version of the truth to win; they want to be holding the crystals — or the bribes, or the IOUs — that the winner will have to buy from them. Their nightmare is not the wrong past surviving. It is the wrong past surviving while they hold no position in it. They intend to cash out a heartbeat before the last pool dries, and they have a clause for every contingency except sentiment.
lore.leadership: The Exchange is run by the Counting House, a rotating quorum of Senior Factors whose authority is measured purely in the size of their book. Pre-eminent among them is the Iodine Comptroller, Vael Surr-of-the-Open-Ledger, who is said to have re-lived so many edited crystals that she remembers seventeen contradictory childhoods and bills the discrepancy to a holding account. She does not give orders; she quotes prices, and a Factor who refuses her price simply discovers that no one in the crew will extend them brine on credit. Below the Counting House, each warband is fronted by a Factor-Captain who funds the operation against future custody — meaning every Factor on the field is technically in debt to their own commander and fighting to clear the balance before the Toll calls it.
lore.homeland: The Factors have no homeland because a homeland is an immobile asset, and the Factors do not hold immobile assets. Their 'territory' is the Salt Exchange itself — a floating, ever-relocating bazaar of lashed skiffs, ledger-barges, and tide-sledges that follows the receding waterline so that it is always moored at the exact margin where fresh crystals are forming. Wherever the brine is leaving fastest, the Exchange is already there, planks down, lamps lit, prices chalked, buying the future before it has finished crystallizing. When a battle ends, the Exchange has already moved on to the next drying flat, leaving nothing behind but chalk-marks and a smell of iodine and coin-cut salt.

signatureRule.name: The Open Ledger
signatureRule.text: The Brine-Factors do not score crystals by holding them — they score by SELLING them. Maintain a single visible pool of Coin (use physical coin-cut salt tokens so the board, not bookkeeping, shows your wealth). EARN: any time a Factor model in base contact with a Loose or Held crystal disengages from it and ends the activation NOT in base contact with that crystal, take the crystal off the board into your Hold and gain 1 Coin — you have liquidated it. A crystal in your Hold is OFF the table: it cannot be shattered, set, or freed by anyone, and it counts as YOUR ontology for the Verdict for as long as it stays in your Hold. SPEND: Coin is the fuel for every other Factor rule — reinforcements, edits, and bribes all cost Coin, and you may spend it the instant a trigger occurs, even in an opponent's activation. The binary decision is constant and brutal: a crystal in your Hold scores and is untouchable, but it is also doing nothing on the board and earning you nothing further — and the moment you spend down to zero Coin you are, in Factor cant, 'liquidated,' and any crystal you take into Hold while at zero Coin must be sold back to the table immediately (placed Loose in the nearest Dry zone). You can never sit on the past. You must keep it moving or it stops paying.

factionSpecialRules.name: Edit the Salt
factionSpecialRules.text: A Factor model in base contact with a Loose or Held crystal may, instead of attacking, spend 1 Coin to Edit it: turn the crystal's objective marker to its reverse face, swapping which faction's ontology it counts as for the Verdict (Fixed becomes Sold, Freed becomes Sold, and so on — a Litany has a defined 'edited' value printed on its card). Instant, binary, visible: the marker is flipped or it isn't, no degrees. An Edited crystal stays Edited until someone else Edits it again or it is Set permanently by a Mnemarch — and a Set crystal can never be Edited, which is the whole reason the Mnemarchs and Factors hate each other. You are not changing what happened. You are changing what it's worth.

factionSpecialRules.name: Working the Angles
factionSpecialRules.text: Once per round, when an opponent declares a charge or a shot targeting one of your models, you may spend 1 Coin to declare that model is Leveraged: it immediately makes a free 'redeploy' move of up to its base Move directly away from the attacker before the attack resolves, and if this carries it out of range or line of sight the attack is wasted. No re-rolls, no to-hit fiddling — the model is simply somewhere else now. You never hold the spot they aimed at. You sold it to them a moment too late.

factionSpecialRules.name: Insurance Clause
factionSpecialRules.text: Every Factor warband opens the game by writing one Policy: name a single enemy unit or a single named Litany on a face-down ledger-stone. The first time that named target is destroyed, shattered, or scored by anyone — friend or foe — you immediately collect on the Policy and gain 2 Coin, no roll, the instant it happens. You profit from the breach you insured. (Factors traditionally insure the Concord Litany's heirs out of sheer professional sentiment.)

factionSpecialRules.name: Bribe the Tide
factionSpecialRules.text: The Factors cannot slow the Long Toll — no faction can — but they can pay to be standing in the right place when it strikes. Once per game, spend 3 Coin at the start of a round, before the Tide marker advances: choose one zone about to flip from Brine-deep to Dry and declare it Underwritten. When it flips Dry this round, every crystal in that zone is taken directly into your Hold (scored and removed) before any Shatter checks can be made against them. You don't stop the water. You just made sure the merchandise was already sold before it got exposed.

subfactions.name: The Skiff-Reaches (the Runners)
subfactions.twist: The fast-money wing — wave-skipping crews who treat the receding tide as a highway and never, ever stop moving. They hold the fewest crystals and earn the most Coin, because they liquidate everything the instant they touch it. Other Factors call them 'thin books': all velocity, no reserves, one bad tide from liquidation.
subfactions.ruleText: Skiff-Reaches models AUTO-PASS the movement penalty of Brine-deep zones — water is a road, not a drag, to them, so they move their full distance whether wet or dry. Additionally, the first time each round a Skiff-Reaches model liquidates a crystal via The Open Ledger, it may immediately make a free Move afterward. Binary: it crossed the water at full speed or it didn't; there is no half-speed wading. They are gone before the splash settles.

subfactions.name: The Counting House (the Brokers)
subfactions.twist: The deep-pockets wing — slow, lavishly-funded ledger-barges and their bodyguard-clerks who don't chase crystals; they buy them off whoever already grabbed them. They are the Factors who win battles in the opponent's deployment zone with a chalk price and a smile. Where the Runners liquidate, the Brokers accumulate Coin until they can simply purchase the outcome.
subfactions.ruleText: At the start of your activation, a Counting House model in base contact with any enemy model that is currently Holding a crystal may spend 3 Coin to Buy the Out: the enemy model immediately drops that crystal as Loose in its own zone (it 'took the deal'), and you gain nothing but the open crystal — which any of your models, including this one, may then liquidate normally. Instant, binary, visible: the crystal is dropped or it isn't. You did not fight them for it. You made them an offer their book couldn't refuse.

subfactions.name: The Iodine Cartel (the Forgers)
subfactions.twist: The disreputable wing even other Factors won't sit downwind of — memory-forgers, iodine-blind to a one, who don't trade real crystals so much as manufacture convincing fakes. They re-live edited memories so often they've forgotten which past is real, and they've decided that's an asset. They specialize in Editing, salting the board with counterfeit history until no one can price the truth.
subfactions.ruleText: Iodine Cartel models pay only 1 Coin to Edit the Salt at any range up to 6 inches instead of needing base contact — they forge from a distance, on the air, the way they forge everything. Once per game, a Cartel model may instead spend 2 Coin to Edit a crystal into a Counterfeit: place a duplicate objective marker (use a spare) in an adjacent Dry zone. The Counterfeit is a real, scorable crystal for the Verdict until the moment ANY faction tries to Set, Free, or Shatter it — at which point it is revealed as fake and removed with no effect, and the would-be actor wasted their entire activation on a lie. Binary: it's real until it's tested, then it never was.

unitConcepts.name: Cutpurse Wavewalkers
unitConcepts.flavor: Lightly-armed runners in oilskin and salt-cracked boots who skim the shallows on bladed wading-poles, here to touch a crystal and be three zones away before anyone reacts. They don't fight for the prize; they relocate it to the Hold and bill you for the inconvenience.

unitConcepts.name: Skiff-Reach Corsairs
unitConcepts.flavor: Wave-skipping raiders riding lashed-plank skiffs with brass-shod prows, treating the receding brine as open road. They strike the flank, liquidate whatever the front line was guarding, and are gone across water no one else can cross at speed.

unitConcepts.name: Factor-Clerks of the Open Book
unitConcepts.flavor: Bespectacled accountants in ink-teal sashes who carry the warband's ledger-stone into the field, chalking prices on the air. They never throw a punch; they Edit the salt under your feet and watch your victory revalue to a loss in their margins.

unitConcepts.name: Ironbound Bodyguard-Clerks
unitConcepts.flavor: Patinaed-brass enforcers in scale-coats whose only job is to keep a Broker's Coin walking and breathing. Slow for a Factor, immovable by Factor standards — a wall of ledger-armor around the wallet, debt-collectors who collect in person.

unitConcepts.name: The Iodine-Blind
unitConcepts.flavor: Hollow-eyed forgers who reek of crystallizing memory, scattering counterfeit Litanies across the flat. They can no longer tell their own past from yours and have monetized the confusion, salting the board with lies until the truth has no quotable price.

unitConcepts.name: The Hauler-Sledge
unitConcepts.role: Heavy support / mobile Hold / objective denial
unitConcepts.flavor: A groaning tide-sledge of lashed barrels and salvage-claws that scoops crystals off the flat by the armful and carries them off-table into the Hold. A rolling vault — slow, greedy, and impossible to rob, because the merchandise is already gone.

unitConcepts.name: Vael Surr, the Iodine Comptroller
unitConcepts.flavor: The pre-eminent Senior Factor, who remembers seventeen childhoods and bills the discrepancy to a holding account. She does not command; she quotes, and the flat reprices around her. She intends to be the last solvent thing the Sea ever sees.

unitConcepts.name: The Auctioneer-Adept
unitConcepts.flavor: A theatrical Broker with a salt-glass gavel and a voice that carries across a drying flat, calling the price on every contested crystal. Wherever the Auctioneer stands, the past goes to the highest bidder — and the bidding never stops until the Toll.

characters.name: Vael Surr, the Iodine Comptroller
characters.title: Faction Warlord / Coin Generator / Market-Controller

uniqueRule.name: Quote the Price
uniqueRule.text: Vael does not give orders; she quotes. At the start of each round, before activations, gain 1 Coin (she has appraised the morning's market). Once per round, when ANY model — friendly or enemy — liquidates, Edits, or Sets a crystal within 9" of Vael, you may immediately gain 1 Coin: she takes her cut of every transaction on the flat. Binary, instant, visible: the deal happened in range or it didn't. While Vael is alive you may spend Coin during an opponent's activation even at zero Coin once per game, going to -1 (a single line of credit); you must return to 0 or positive by the end of your next activation or Vael is Liquidated and removed as a casualty — the only thing that can kill the Comptroller is her own book.

characters.flavor: She remembers seventeen childhoods and bills the discrepancy to a holding account — and intends to be the last solvent thing the Sea ever sees.

characters.name: The Auctioneer-Adept
characters.title: Hero Support / Tempo-Control / Bribe Specialist

uniqueRule.name: Going Once, Going Twice
uniqueRule.text: Once per round, the Auctioneer may Call the Lot: choose one Loose or Held crystal within 12" and line of sight. Until the Auctioneer's next activation, the FIRST friendly model to liquidate that named crystal earns 1 extra Coin (it went to the highest bidder). Additionally, you may spend 2 Coin during an enemy activation, when an enemy model is about to liquidate, Set, Free, or Shatter the Called crystal, to Outbid: that action is cancelled and the model's activation ends — they were talked out of it at the rostrum. Binary, instant, visible: the lot is Called or it isn't; the bid is paid or it isn't. No to-hit fiddling, no stacking — the gavel falls once.

characters.flavor: Wherever the Auctioneer stands the past goes to the highest bidder, and the bidding never stops until the Toll strikes dry.

factions.name: The Sediment (the Re-Dreaming)
factions.battleCry: "Let it go. Let it ALL go — and walk back out of the salt with us."

lore.origin: The Sediment was not founded; it accreted. Where the other three orders crystallized around scholars, zealots, and merchants — people with names and signatures — the Sediment began the first time a wading archivist died on the flat and the tide, receding past her body, declined to erase her. She rose. Salt-skinned, translucent, remembering nothing but the single moment that held her solid, she walked toward the nearest pool as if drawn to a hearth. The hierophants of the Sediment are the rare living few who watched this happen and understood it not as horror but as mercy: Veyl had refused to finish a grief, and so the grieved-for had been spared the worse fate of never having been. The order's true founders are therefore the Reliquiae themselves, and the living merely keep the doors open. Their oldest doctrine is a single overheard sentence — believed to be the god's, half-dreamed up out of a drying pool by an iodine-blind hermit: 'I am so tired of holding them.' The Sediment took it as instruction.
lore.culture: They have no archives, because to archive is to fix, and to fix is to refuse the god its rest. Instead they keep middens — sprawling, deliberately disorganized heaps of un-set salt-glass left loose in the wet so the tide can take any of it at any time. A Sediment camp is identifiable by the absence of locks, walls, and ledgers, and by the constant low chorus of the salt-dead murmuring the one moment each can still remember, over and over, until the sound becomes a kind of weather. The living among them practice 'thinning': deliberately re-living crystals until they go iodine-blind, surrendering the boundary between their own past and the Sea's, because a hierophant who can no longer tell whose memory is whose can speak to the Reliquiae as kin. They do not mourn their dead. They greet them. A Sediment funeral is a welcome party held in advance.
lore.whyTheyFight: They do not fight to win the past. They fight to ensure no one else fixes it, because every Set crystal is a thought the god is forbidden to release — a splinter driven into a dying mind to keep it awake and in pain. The Mnemarchs call this preservation; the Sediment calls it the cruelest thing in the world. Their war aim is not victory but completion: they want the Long Toll to strike Dry with as much history as possible still loose, dissolving, free to return to solution and to silence. Where the Iconoclasts shatter crystals to deny them — an act of violence the Sediment finds vulgar and incomplete, because a shattered moment is still a moment that was forcibly ended — the Sediment simply lets the tide do its work, and protects the tide's right to do it. To them, a crystal that dissolves back into the brine was never lost. It went home.
lore.leadership: There is no hierarch, because hierarchy is a structure and structures are fixed. The Sediment is led, loosely and reluctantly, by the Grief-Touched: living hierophants so deep into iodine-blindness that they have begun to weep brine and shed salt at the fingertips, halfway to becoming Reliquiae themselves. The eldest of these is called the Undertow — a title, not a name, because whoever holds it has forgotten their name on purpose. The Undertow does not give orders so much as point at a drying pool and start walking, trusting the swarm to understand. Beneath the Grief-Touched, the Reliquiae organize themselves by the era of the moment that holds them: the salt-dead of older memories defer to those of newer ones, on the theory that the freshest grief is the closest to the god's present thought and therefore knows best where it wants to flinch next.
lore.homeland: The Lees — the lowest, oldest, most thoroughly evaporated quarter of the Litany Sea, where the brine receded first and the salt lies deepest. It is a sunken plain of fossil tide-lines, ankle-deep where it is wet at all, studded with the standing salt-figures of Reliquiae who walked there in ages past and simply stopped, too far from any pool to stay solid, frozen mid-stride forever. The living call it the boneyard; the Sediment calls it the Nursery, because the Lees is where the god has done its most thorough forgetting, and the air there is so thick with iodine that the boundary between memory and self dissolves on the first breath. No other faction will hold ground in the Lees. The salt-dead are too many, the pools too few, and the murmuring never, ever stops.

subfactions.name: The Undertow Choir
subfactions.twist: The orthodox Sediment — the swarm at its purest. They believe the Reliquiae should never be commanded, only invited, and so they fight by opening the way and letting the salt-dead pour through it. The Choir runs the largest middens and the deepest iodine-blindness; their living members are barely living at all, and they are the only Sediment cell that has Grief-Touched in genuine command. Their twist is generosity weaponized: the Choir actively floods its own zones and shatters its own un-set salt-glass to feed the Grief pool faster, treating its history as kindling for the horde.
subfactions.ruleText: At the start of each round, before the Toll advances, the Choir may voluntarily shatter one Loose salt-glass crystal it controls in a Brine-deep zone. If it does, immediately add 1 token to the Grief pool, AND every Reliquia Re-dreamed this round may be placed in a Brine-deep zone instead of only Dry zones — AUTO, no roll. This is a binary choice each round: spend your own history to put the swarm where it cannot be shattered.

subfactions.name: The Lees-Walkers
subfactions.twist: Hardliners from the Nursery who reject even the Undertow's gentleness. They do not wait for the tide to free the past — they go and stand on Set crystals until the god, flinching at the desecration of its own enforced memory, weeps them loose. They are the only Sediment who willingly enter Dry zones in force, because the Lees taught them that dryness is not death but the threshold of return. Their twist is that they treat the enemy's permanence as a resource: a Mnemarch Set crystal, to a Lees-Walker, is the richest possible vein of grief, just waiting to be pried open.
subfactions.ruleText: A Lees-Walker model in base contact with an enemy-Set crystal at the start of a round does not move or act normally; instead it Stands Vigil. While at least one model Stands Vigil on a given Set crystal, that crystal counts as Exposed for shatter purposes for ALL factions (its permanence is cracking). This is the only way the Sediment can touch a Set crystal — they cannot un-Set it, but they can re-open it to the Toll and the crossfire. Binary: a Vigil is being stood, or it is not.

subfactions.name: The Brine-Wet Cantors
subfactions.twist: Apostates and recent converts — many of them former Brine-Factors who were edited too many times and lost the thread of their own sales, and ex-Mnemarchs who broke under the weight of all they were forced to keep. They are the Sediment's only mobile, semi-coherent fighting cell, and the rest of the order distrusts them for it, because mobility implies destination and the Sediment believes only in dissolution. Their twist is that they still think like the factions that made them: they manipulate the tide and the Grief pool with a trader's cunning the pure swarm lacks, hastening floods and recessions to bait the enemy into Dry-zone catastrophes.
subfactions.ruleText: Once per game, when the Tide marker is about to flip a band of zones, the Cantors may name one zone in that band and declare it 'Drowned First' or 'Dried First.' That single zone flips one notch ahead of its band (a Brine-deep zone may go Dry now, or stay wet one notch longer). Everyone can see it coming — it is announced — but only the Cantors choose. Use it to strand an enemy crystal in the open, or to keep your own swarm cushioned one tide longer.

signatureRule.name: The Re-Dreaming
signatureRule.text: The Sediment never loses a Reliquia — it only sends one back to be re-remembered. When any Reliquia model is removed as a casualty, do not destroy it: set it aside in the Re-Dreaming pile. At the start of every round, AFTER the Toll advances and zones flip, count the Grief pool. You may spend Grief tokens 1-for-1 to return Reliquiae from the Re-Dreaming pile directly onto the board in any Dry zone — AUTO-RETURN, no roll, no scatter, placed standing and ready. The Grief pool fills from the whole table's violence: every crystal that shatters (yours, theirs, anyone's) and every zone that flips Dry on the Toll adds 1 token, automatically, tied to the visible board. This is the engine and the whole decision of the faction: the more the table degrades — the more the Iconoclasts shatter, the more the Mnemarchs are forced to fight near crystals, the further the Long Toll strikes — the larger your swarm re-dreams. You do not husband your models. You spend them like water, because the drying board pays you back in bodies. The one limit is the tide itself: a Reliquia the receding brine passes over TWICE is truly erased and removed from the Re-Dreaming pile for good — solid only while wet, gone the moment its zone has been Dry across two full tides. Manage that, and you cannot run out of dead.

factionSpecialRules.name: Solid Only While Wet
factionSpecialRules.text: A Reliquia is a moment the god has not finished forgetting, and dryness is forgetting. Track each set-aside Reliquia's zone, not with bookkeeping but with the terrain overlay everyone can already see. A Reliquia standing in a Brine-deep zone when it recedes to Dry is fine — it has been Dry for one tide. If that same model is still in a zone that has been Dry for a SECOND consecutive tide, it is erased: removed from play and from the Re-Dreaming pile, gone for good. The decision this forces: keep your swarm moving toward whatever brine is left, or feed it deliberately into the Dry to die-and-return through the Grief pool before the second tide claims it. Binary, visible, no roll — the overlay tells you which of your dead are about to stop being able to come back.

factionSpecialRules.name: Drown The Prize
factionSpecialRules.text: The Sediment cannot Set crystals and refuses to Edit or sell them — it only wants them loose and dissolving. A Litany or salt-glass crystal that is Held by a Sediment model in a Brine-deep zone at the moment the Long Toll strikes Dry counts as Freed for the Verdict: it dissolved back into the Sea on the Sediment's terms, and scores for them as a returned moment. The catch and the decision: it must be WET when the Toll strikes. The Sediment's whole endgame is dragging the prize into the shrinking water and holding the line with bodies while everyone else tries to pull it out into the lethal Dry — an inversion of every other faction, who want their prizes safely Dry-and-controlled or Set.

factionSpecialRules.name: The Murmuring Tide
factionSpecialRules.text: The constant chorus of the salt-dead unnerves the living. Any non-Sediment model that ends a round in base contact with three or more Reliquiae cannot Run on its next activation — IGNORE its run, it may only make a normal move. Binary on/off, checked against the visible board: surrounded by enough of the murmuring dead, you are slowed by the weight of remembered grief whether you believe in it or not. The swarm doesn't just block ground; standing in it costs you tempo.

factionSpecialRules.name: Welcome, Not Mourning
factionSpecialRules.text: The Sediment treats its Grief-Touched leaders as already half-gone, and their fall only hastens a homecoming. When a Sediment Grief-Touched model (any hierophant-type leader) is removed as a casualty, immediately add 3 tokens to the Grief pool instead of the usual 1 — the god flinches hard at the loss of one who was nearly its own. There is no morale penalty, no command range collapsing, no panic: the swarm does not need a living voice to know where the water is going. Killing a Sediment leader feeds the Re-Dreaming. The decision lands on your opponent: cutting the head off this faction only makes the body larger.

unitConcepts.name: Wadeling Drift
unitConcepts.flavor: The freshly-risen — Reliquiae of recent, shallow deaths, still wearing the salt-fused rags of whoever they were a tide ago. They wade in loose drifts toward the nearest pool, drowning crystals in sheer translucent numbers, and they are the cheapest, most numerous re-dreaming in the order. Each one remembers exactly one moment, and murmurs it without pause until it is removed and re-remembered. They do not fear death because they have already met it and found it survivable.

unitConcepts.name: Tide-Drowned Bulwark
unitConcepts.flavor: Old Reliquiae of deep, ancient deaths from the Lees, grown thick and barnacled with accreted salt-glass until they are nearly statues that walk. They plant themselves in the wet and refuse to leave, cushioning crystals beneath them and daring the Dry to come and take them. Slow, near-immovable, and impossible to truly kill while the water holds — the living wall the swarm builds around a Drowned prize.

unitConcepts.name: The Undertow (Grief-Touched Hierophant)
unitConcepts.flavor: The order's reluctant head, weeping brine from blind eyes and shedding salt from fingertips already going translucent — a living person dissolving into a Reliquia in real time, and welcoming it. The Undertow gives no orders, only walks toward the drying pools the god most wants emptied, and the swarm follows because they can hear, in the murmur, that it is right. When it finally falls, the Grief it sheds re-dreams a tide of the dead in its place.

unitConcepts.name: Lees-Walker Vigilants
unitConcepts.flavor: Zealots from the Nursery who march into the lethal Dry on purpose to stand vigil atop the enemy's Set crystals, cracking the god's enforced permanence open by their mere desecrating presence. Salt-crusted to the knees from the boneyard, indifferent to the crossfire, they exist to make the Mnemarchs' untouchable prizes touchable again — and to die doing it, knowing the Grief pool will simply hand them back.

unitConcepts.name: Brine-Wet Cantor
unitConcepts.flavor: An apostate from another order — a ledger-blind ex-Factor or a broken ex-Mnemarch — who still thinks with a heretic's cunning the pure swarm lacks. The Cantor reads the Long Toll like a trader reads a market, naming which zone drowns or dries ahead of its band to strand an enemy crystal or cushion the dead one tide longer. The Sediment distrusts them and uses them anyway, because someone has to point the flood.

unitConcepts.name: Murmur-Host
unitConcepts.flavor: Not a unit so much as a tide of Reliquiae moving as one chorus, packed shoulder to translucent shoulder, their overlapping murmurs thickening into a sound the living cannot move quickly through. The Murmur-Host doesn't fight; it occupies, smothering whole zones in slowed, grieving bodies until the enemy's tempo drowns. Where it stands, no one runs.

unitConcepts.name: Standing Salt (Erasure-Born)
unitConcepts.flavor: The largest re-dreamings — Reliquiae of moments so vast or so violently shattered that the god's flinch returns them outsized and terrible, half-formed and crackling with un-set memory. They surge up from the Re-Dreaming pile only when the Grief pool runs deep, the board's own decay made flesh: the more the table has died, the bigger the thing that walks back out of the salt. A living embodiment of the corruption-scaling promise.

unitConcepts.name: The Stranded
unitConcepts.flavor: Reliquiae deliberately fed into the deep Dry, far from any brine, racing the second tide that will erase them forever. They strike where no one expects the dead to reach, knowing they have one tide to act before they are truly gone — a suicide-runner with nothing to lose and one last moment to spend. Used right, they trade a permanently-lost model for a prize no one thought the Sediment could touch.
